newsitem.title: GEORGIA: Georgia parliament mulls impeaching security chief.
newsitem.headline: Georgia parliament mulls impeaching security chief.

text.p: Georgia's parliament prepared to vote on Friday whether to begin impeachment proceedings against Security Minister Shota Kviraya.

He is accused by a group of lawmakers of executing six suspected looters during a 1993 civil war, authorising the bugging of telephones of several journalists and working for Russian intelligence services.
Kviraya vigorously denied all charges in a letter published in a Georgian newspaper earlier this week.
A total of 79, or one-third of all deputies, needed to vote in favour of starting impeachment proceedings for the complicated process to begin.

A parallel resolution will ask President Eduard Shevardnadze to temporarily remove Kviraya from duty while his fate is decided. Shevardnadze said earlier this week that even if some of the charges are true, the minister should be removed from office.

The Supreme Court would then have to consider the validity of the request before full parliamentary impeachment hearings could begin. A majority of lawmakers would then need to vote for impeachment for him to be dismissed.
Parliament met in closed session late on Thursday night to consider the charges against the minister.

Mikhail Osadze, head of a parliamentary investigation commission, told reporters that video footage existed which showed Kviraya personally executing six alleged looters with a pistol in the western city of Zugdidi near the end of the country's last civil war in 1993.
The footage was not immediately available to journalists.
At the time, Kviraya was Interior Minister.

Irina Sarishvili, leader of the centre-right National Democratic Party who has spearheaded the drive against Kviraya, told reporters the minister had admitted in the session to authorising phone taps of several leading journalists.
"He said that in some cases the telephone eavesdropping had been legal," Sarishvili-Chanturia said.
She said Kviraya claimed not to have approved some of the bugging incidents and that in those cases members of the security apparatus responsible for them had been dismissed.
Kviraya later left the session with chest pains, deputies said.
